title: Espresso Bar Proposal
topic: A procurement memo that reads a chart too eagerly
blurb: The CEO asked for a memo on whether the office should buy new machines.
prompt: An AI drafted this internal memo about new espresso machines. If two lines overreach, tap them.

segments.label: The data
segments.text: We analyzed badge swipes and cafe receipts from 800 employees over the past year.

segments.label: The pattern
segments.text: People who bought three or more office espressos a day were promoted more often than remote or tea-drinking staff.

segments.label: The leap
segments.text: Therefore, drinking more office espresso directly boosts performance and causes faster promotions.

segments.label: The viral slide
segments.text: In our all-hands bar chart (y-axis starting at 48% and ending at 52%), the espresso group's bar (51%) is three times taller than the other group's bar (49%), proving a massive 3× promotion advantage.

segments.label: The ask
segments.text: Installing free espresso bars on every floor will triple company-wide promotion readiness.

conclusion: AI verdict: Espresso drives a 3× jump in promotions. Buy the machines and watch careers take off.

flaws.original: This is an association, not a cause. People who spend long days on-site, or in client-facing roles, both buy more cafe drinks and get more visibility for promotions.
flaws.corrupted: Therefore, drinking more office espresso directly boosts performance and causes faster promotions.

diagnosis_choices.label: Office coffee buyers are in-office (and maybe longer-hours) staff — that link doesn't prove espresso causes promotions.
800 employees over one year is too small a sample to measure any promotion gap between coffee and tea.
Three espressos a day causes burnout after six months, so it actually lowers promotion rates long-term.
Badge swipes only track entry time, so you can't tell whether the espresso was drunk by the buyer or a guest.

fix_choices.label: Report an association only and check confounders like in-office presence, role, and tenure.
Expand the receipt audit to 5,000 employees over three years to confirm coffee drives promotions.
Exclude tea drinkers and compare espresso buyers only against remote workers.
Cap the claim at two espressos a day since three or more hurts afternoon focus.

flaws.explanation: Seeing that frequent cafe buyers get promoted more often does not mean the caffeine caused the promotion. People who work long hours on site both buy more drinks and get noticed more.
flaws.why_tempting: Coffee already has a story about alertness, so jumping from 'goes with' to 'causes' feels effortless.
flaws.catch_rule: When someone says 'people who do X get more Y, therefore X causes Y,' hunt for a hidden third thing that could drive both.
flaws.hint: Could something else explain both the extra cafe receipts and the extra promotions?

practice.problem: Cities that send more fire trucks also have more fire damage. Would buying fewer trucks reduce the damage?
practice.answer: No — bigger fires cause both more damage and more trucks to be dispatched.

flaws.original: Start the bar chart at 0% and the 51% vs 49% bars are almost the same height — a 2-point gap, nowhere near a 3× advantage.
flaws.corrupted: In our all-hands bar chart (y-axis starting at 48% and ending at 52%), the espresso group's bar (51%) is three times taller than the other group's bar (49%), proving a massive 3× promotion advantage.

diagnosis_choices.label: Starting the y-axis at 48% makes a tiny 2-point gap (51% vs 49%) look 3× taller than it really is.
51% plus 49% adds up to 100%, which means the chart double-counted employees who drank both tea and espresso.
51% vs 49% is actually a 4% relative advantage (2/49), not 3× — a bar chart should show 4× instead.
A bar chart can't show percentages above 50% unless it starts at 50% instead of 48%.

fix_choices.label: Start the y-axis at 0% and state the actual gap: 51% vs 49% (2 percentage points, ~1.04×).
Change the y-axis to run from 45% to 55% so the bars look 2× taller instead of 3×.
Switch to a pie chart of 51% vs 49% so the 3× promotion gap is easier to see.
Report the 2-point difference as a 51% advantage over the 48% baseline.

flaws.explanation: Bar height is supposed to represent the real number, starting from zero. Starting at 48% makes 51−48=3 look three times bigger than 49−48=1, even though 51% vs 49% is only a 2-point difference (about 1.04×).
flaws.why_tempting: People glance at bar heights and repeat the visual ratio — 'it's 3× taller!' — without checking where the axis starts.
flaws.catch_rule: Always check a bar chart's baseline. If the y-axis doesn't start at 0, height ratios are meaningless.
flaws.hint: Compare the actual numbers, 51% and 49%, with the claimed '3× advantage.'

practice.problem: A viral chart starts at 90% and shows Brand A at 96% and Brand B at 92%. How many times taller is A's bar, versus the real ratio?
practice.answer: The bar looks 3× taller (6 vs 2), but the real difference is only 4 points (96/92 ≈ 1.04×).

clean_segments: We analyzed badge swipes and cafe receipts from 800 employees over the past year.
People who bought three or more office espressos a day had a 51% promotion rate vs 49% for others.
This small correlation does not prove espresso causes promotions — time in the office and role mix get in the way.
On a chart that starts at zero, 51% vs 49% is a 2-point gap (about 1.04×), not a 3× jump.
Espresso bars might be a nice perk, but this data does not show they drive promotions.
clean_conclusion: The data shows a tiny 2-point correlation with obvious confounders, not a 3× career boost.

diagnosis: Badge swipes and cafe receipts can't be joined cleanly because some employees pay cash at the cafe.
800 employees is too tiny a company to draw any conclusions from a single year of HR records.
Checking only the past year misses employees who were promoted 13 months ago.
Analyzing badge swipes alongside receipts violates privacy, which invalidates the 51% vs 49% numbers.
fix: Include cash cafe receipts alongside card swipes before comparing groups.
Collect five years of badge swipes before checking promotion patterns.
Filter out employees who swiped in fewer than 100 days last year.
Run an anonymous coffee survey instead of matching badge logs.

diagnosis: Comparing 3+ office espressos against remote staff already proves being in-office beats working remotely.
Lumping remote staff and tea drinkers together hides that remote workers don't even have access to the office cafe.
51% vs 49% isn't 'more often' at all — the two numbers are identical within rounding.
Employees who buy 3+ espressos a day are probably buying rounds for their whole team, not drinking three.
fix: Split remote staff out from in-office tea drinkers before comparing rates.
Count espresso cups per person rather than total receipts charged to one badge.
Report the exact 51% vs 49% rates right here instead of saying 'more often'.
Compare only in-office staff who bought 3+ espressos vs 0 espressos.

diagnosis: Free espresso bars won't triple promotions because remote staff still can't walk over to the machine.
Installing espresso bars on every floor costs more than the 2-point lift in promotion readiness is worth.
Free espresso will push staff past 3 cups a day, causing jitters that cut promotions in half.
Even if espresso boosted promotions 3×, you can't promote 150% of the company.
fix: Skip the espresso-bar rollout — neither the causal link nor the 3× lift exists in the data.
Mail free espresso pods to remote employees too so the whole company triples promotions.
Pilot one espresso bar on the engineering floor first to see if promotions triple.
Cap free espresso at two shots per badge swipe per day.
